Six questions, one transparent investigation

Filters update descriptive charts only. Grades are on a 0–20 scale. Hover over marks for values; tables provide accessible chart data.

From comparisons to adjusted associations

The prespecified OLS model adjusts for study-time category, internet access, parental education, age, sex, school, previous failures, absences and higher-education plans. Intervals use HC3 heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors. This is an exploratory association model; adjustment does not establish causation.

Can we predict outcomes without earlier grades?

Methods & limitations

Historical observational data from two Portuguese secondary schools, described in Cortez & Silva (2008). The Portuguese-language file contains 649 records and 33 columns. School reports supply grades; questionnaires supply background information. This is not a representative national survey or a measure of student satisfaction.

Box plots show median, interquartile range, 1.5×IQR whiskers and outliers. Comparison charts show means with 95% percentile bootstrap intervals (5,000 resamples, seed 42) for the full dataset. Filtered groups use approximate 95% t intervals. These intervals describe sampling variability under independent observations; they do not account for school clustering. Two schools are insufficient for reliable cluster inference. Heatmap cells with fewer than 10 records are suppressed.

Zero grades are retained. Absence counts may not capture all disengagement. Small groups, confounding, reverse causation and multiple exploratory comparisons limit inference. Support recipients may have needed help before receiving it. No claim is made that support reduces achievement. There are no survey weights. Do not use the model to make decisions about individual students.
